subject: Global Perspectives
title: Stage 8 Global Perspectives Placement Exam
description: Show what you remember from Stages 1 to 7 so we can find your perfect starting point.
attemptsAllowed: Unlimited — this exam finds your starting point; it is never a fail
feedbackMode: Immediate child-friendly feedback with a placement report

ready.label: Ready for Stage 8
ready.message: Brilliant work! You remember your earlier Global Perspectives skills well. Stage 8, here you come.

readyWithReview.label: Ready — with a little review
readyWithReview.message: You are ready to start Stage 8. Warm up first with the review lessons below.

notReady.label: Let's build strong roots first

sections.title: Stage 7 skills
sections.description: The six Stage 7 thinking skills in action: planning research, analysing causes and perspectives, evaluating sources and arguments, reflecting on your learning, working in a team and communicating your findings.

sections.title: Stage 6 skills
sections.description: Key Stage 6 skills: sorting local, national and global issues, reading charts for patterns, checking who made a source and why, balanced reflection, building on teammates' ideas and stating a clear position.

sections.title: Foundations (Stage 4)
sections.description: The first steps of every skill from Stage 4: collecting answers to a question, reading a tally chart, telling facts from opinions, reflecting, sharing tasks fairly and presenting clearly.

questions.question: Amal wants to find out how the long dry season affects families in her town. What should she do first?
questions.options: Ask a friend to guess the answer for her | Design a colourful poster of her findings | Write one clear research question she wants to answer | Copy the first website she finds into her notebook
questions.correctAnswer: Write one clear research question she wants to answer
questions.explanation: Every good investigation starts with a clear research question. The question guides which sources, methods and evidence Amal will need.

questions.question: Amal is researching water shortages in her town. Which of these is a primary source?
questions.options: An interview she records with a local farmer | An encyclopedia entry about the water cycle | A textbook chapter about droughts in general | A friend's summary of a news article
questions.correctAnswer: An interview she records with a local farmer
questions.explanation: A primary source is first-hand information collected directly, like an interview. Textbooks, encyclopedias and summaries are secondary sources made from other people's information.

questions.question: Yusuf's research question is 'How does drought affect food prices in his region?' Which set of search keywords will find the most useful results?
questions.options: food I like to eat | drought food prices region | how does weather work | interesting facts for school projects
questions.correctAnswer: drought food prices region
questions.explanation: Good search keywords are the most important words from your research question. Extra words like 'interesting' or off-topic words bring back pages that do not answer the question.

questions.question: Hodan wants to know what one hundred students at her school think about a new lunch menu. Which research method fits best?
questions.options: A short questionnaire that every student can fill in | Watching one lunch table for a day | A one-hour interview with a single student | Reading a book about food around the world
questions.correctAnswer: A short questionnaire that every student can fill in
questions.explanation: A questionnaire collects the same questions from many people quickly, so it is the best method when you want the views of a large group.

questions.question: Layla is making a cause and consequence map about plastic rubbish in the river. Which of these belongs in a consequence box?
questions.options: Shops give out free plastic bags | Fish in the river are harmed by the plastic | People drop litter on the riverbank | There are few rubbish bins near the river
questions.correctAnswer: Fish in the river are harmed by the plastic
questions.explanation: A consequence is a result that happens because of the issue. Free bags, few bins and dropped litter are causes; harmed fish is what happens as a result.

questions.question: A farmer and a factory owner disagree about building a new dam on the river. What best explains why they disagree?
questions.options: They see the issue from different perspectives shaped by their own lives | Dams are impossible to have opinions about | They have not read the same book | One of them must be lying about the dam
questions.correctAnswer: They see the issue from different perspectives shaped by their own lives
questions.explanation: A perspective is a way of seeing an issue shaped by a person's situation. The farmer worries about water for crops and the owner about power for the factory — both can be honest and still disagree.

questions.question: Layla is studying the issue 'the local well ran dry'. Which of these belongs in a cause box on her map?
questions.options: Families now walk far to fetch water | Much less rain fell this year than usual | The school garden dried up | Water sellers raised their prices
questions.correctAnswer: Much less rain fell this year than usual
questions.explanation: A cause happens before the issue and helps make it happen. Less rain led to the dry well; the long walks, dry garden and higher prices are consequences that came after.

questions.question: A poster says: 'Everyone in our town wants the new road.' When Layla analyses this claim, what weakness should she spot?
questions.options: It speaks for every person without giving any evidence | It uses the word 'town', which is not allowed | It talks about a road instead of a school | It is too short to be a real sentence
questions.correctAnswer: It speaks for every person without giving any evidence
questions.explanation: Careful analysts notice sweeping words like 'everyone'. Without evidence such as a survey, the claim cannot really speak for the whole town.

questions.question: Tariq is sorting statements into facts and opinions. Which of these is an opinion?
questions.options: Our school has two football pitches | Football is the most enjoyable sport to watch | Eleven players from each team are on the pitch | The match on Friday starts at four o'clock
questions.correctAnswer: Football is the most enjoyable sport to watch
questions.explanation: An opinion tells you what someone feels or believes and cannot be proved true for everyone. The other statements can be checked, so they are facts.

questions.question: Tariq finds four sources about a health story. Which one should he trust most?
questions.options: A national health organisation's report that shows its evidence | A five-year-old forum post by an unknown user | A blog post whose author is not named | An advert for a new health drink
questions.correctAnswer: A national health organisation's report that shows its evidence
questions.explanation: A trustworthy source comes from experts, shows where its evidence comes from and is up to date. Unnamed authors, adverts and old forum posts fail those checks.

questions.question: Tariq reads: 'We should plant more trees in town, because they give shade and clean the air.' In this argument, what is 'because they give shade and clean the air'?
questions.options: The claim the writer wants us to accept | An opinion with nothing to do with trees | The reasons given to support the claim | The conclusion of a science experiment
questions.correctAnswer: The reasons given to support the claim
questions.explanation: An argument has a claim and reasons. 'We should plant more trees' is the claim, and the part after 'because' gives the reasons that support it.

questions.question: Before judging an argument about banning cars from the market street, Tariq fills in a strengths-and-weaknesses grid. Why is this a good habit?
questions.options: It proves the argument is wrong before he reads it | It shows him which side his friends are on | It lets him skip reading the argument carefully | It makes him weigh the good points and weak points before deciding
questions.correctAnswer: It makes him weigh the good points and weak points before deciding
questions.explanation: Good evaluators look at both sides of an argument fairly. The grid slows you down so your judgement rests on the argument's real strengths and weaknesses, not on your first feeling.

questions.question: Maryam has just finished a research project. Which question will help her reflect on it most deeply?
questions.options: Did my friends finish their projects too? | What would I do differently next time, and why? | How quickly can I start the next project? | Which pen did I use for the title page?
questions.correctAnswer: What would I do differently next time, and why?
questions.explanation: Reflection means looking back at your learning to improve. Asking what you would change, and why, turns the finished project into a lesson for the next one.

questions.question: Maryam used to think bottled water was always safest, but the evidence she collected changed her mind. What should she record in her reflection journal?
questions.options: How her viewpoint changed and which evidence changed it | A list of classmates who agree with her new view | Nothing, because changing your mind is a mistake | Only her old viewpoint, to stay consistent
questions.correctAnswer: How her viewpoint changed and which evidence changed it
questions.explanation: Changing your mind because of good evidence is a strength, not a mistake. A reflection journal captures the before, the after and the evidence that made the difference.

questions.question: Which of these journal sentences shows genuine reflection, rather than just a list of what happened?
questions.options: I found interviews hard, so next time I will prepare my questions earlier | My project had six pages and a cover | On Monday I did the interview and on Tuesday I wrote it up | I handed my project in on time
questions.correctAnswer: I found interviews hard, so next time I will prepare my questions earlier
questions.explanation: Real reflection judges how the learning went and plans an improvement. The other sentences only describe what happened without thinking about it.

questions.question: A team of four is starting a project about safe roads. What is the best way to divide the work?
questions.options: Give all the boring jobs to the newest member | Wait and see who feels like working on the day | Agree roles that match each member's strengths and share the work fairly | Let the fastest writer do everything alone
questions.correctAnswer: Agree roles that match each member's strengths and share the work fairly
questions.explanation: Strong teams talk about their strengths first, then agree roles so every member has a fair, clear job. That way nobody is overloaded and nobody is left out.

questions.question: Which of these habits would harm a project team?
questions.options: Members listen to each other's suggestions | Members thank each other for finished tasks | The team checks its plan together each week | One person makes every decision without asking the others
questions.correctAnswer: One person makes every decision without asking the others
questions.explanation: Teams work best when decisions are shared. When one person decides everything alone, other members stop contributing their ideas and effort.

questions.question: Hassan disagrees with his teammate's idea for the project poster. What should he do?
questions.options: Tell the rest of the team the idea is stupid | Explain his reasons politely and listen to his teammate's reasons too | Leave the team and work alone | Stay silent and complain about the poster later
questions.correctAnswer: Explain his reasons politely and listen to his teammate's reasons too
questions.explanation: Disagreement is normal in teams. Sharing your reasons respectfully, and really listening to the other side, helps the team choose the best idea together.

questions.question: Arjun presented his water-saving findings to the town council. Next week he presents the same findings to young children. What should he change?
questions.options: Use simpler words and more pictures to suit his new audience | Nothing, because a presentation never changes | Only the colour of his shirt | The findings themselves, so they sound more exciting
questions.correctAnswer: Use simpler words and more pictures to suit his new audience
questions.explanation: Good communicators match their language and style to their audience and purpose. The findings stay honest and the same; the way of sharing them changes.

questions.question: Arjun plans his talk with an introduction, a body and a conclusion. What belongs in the conclusion?
questions.options: A joke that has nothing to do with the talk | All of his evidence, explained for the first time | A short summary of his main message | A brand-new topic he has not mentioned
questions.correctAnswer: A short summary of his main message
questions.explanation: The conclusion reminds the audience of the main message so it stays in their minds. New topics and first-time evidence belong in the body, not the ending.

questions.question: Arjun wants his talk to persuade people to save water. What is the strongest way to build his argument?
questions.options: State a clear claim and support it with evidence | Say that anyone who disagrees is wrong | List facts about oceans that are not about saving water | Repeat the same sentence ten times, louder each time
questions.correctAnswer: State a clear claim and support it with evidence
questions.explanation: A persuasive argument is a clear claim held up by evidence. Shouting, insulting other views or drifting off topic weakens a talk instead of strengthening it.

questions.question: Communication has two halves: sharing your ideas and listening to others. While a classmate presents, what does a good communicator do?
questions.options: Look at the clock until it is their turn | Interrupt whenever they disagree | Listen carefully and note questions to ask at the end | Practise their own talk out loud at the same time
questions.correctAnswer: Listen carefully and note questions to ask at the end
questions.explanation: Listening is half of communication. Careful listeners understand the speaker's ideas and ask thoughtful questions at the right moment.

questions.question: Sagal is sorting issues by size. How should she sort 'a broken tap in the school corridor'?
questions.options: A local issue | A global issue | Not an issue at all | A national issue
questions.correctAnswer: A local issue
questions.explanation: A local issue affects one place, like a school or a neighbourhood. National issues affect a whole country, and global issues affect many countries.

questions.question: Sagal wants to know exactly how much rain fell in her town last month. Which source should she choose?
questions.options: A poster advertising umbrellas | A story about a rainy day | The weather office's rainfall records | Her neighbour's memory of wet days
questions.correctAnswer: The weather office's rainfall records
questions.explanation: When you need exact numbers, choose a source whose job is to measure and record them. Memories, stories and adverts are not reliable for measurements.

questions.question: A chart shows the rubbish collected at the beach clean-up each month: 20 bags, then 26, then 31, then 38. What pattern does the chart show?
questions.options: The amount of rubbish is falling month by month | The amount of rubbish is rising month by month | The amount of rubbish stays exactly the same | The chart shows no pattern at all
questions.correctAnswer: The amount of rubbish is rising month by month
questions.explanation: Reading numbers in order shows the pattern: 20, 26, 31, 38 goes up every month. Spotting patterns like this is how analysts turn data into meaning.

questions.question: Khadra does a one-minute check on a website before trusting it. Which two questions should she ask first?
questions.options: Is the website's name easy to spell, and is it short? | How many pictures does it have, and are they pretty? | Who made this source, and why did they make it? | Do my friends like it, and does it load quickly?
questions.correctAnswer: Who made this source, and why did they make it?
questions.explanation: Knowing who made a source and why tells you whether it is there to inform you, persuade you or sell to you — the heart of judging whether to trust it.

questions.question: Khadra is studying an advert for a new fruit juice. What is the main purpose of an advert?
questions.options: To persuade people to buy something | To report news with no side at all | To test people's reading skills | To teach people the whole truth about a topic
questions.correctAnswer: To persuade people to buy something
questions.explanation: Every source has a purpose. An advert's purpose is to sell, so it shows only the good side — a careful evaluator remembers that when reading its claims.

questions.question: After a group project, Liban writes a personal reflection. What should a balanced reflection include?
questions.options: Just the marks he hopes to get | Only the parts that went well | Both what went well and what was difficult | Only the parts that went badly
questions.correctAnswer: Both what went well and what was difficult
questions.explanation: A balanced reflection looks honestly at both sides — the successes to keep and the difficulties to work on. That is how reflection leads to real improvement.

questions.question: In a team meeting, Liban wants to build on a teammate's suggestion. Which sentence starter should he use?
questions.options: That is wrong, listen to my idea instead | I was not listening, can we move on? | I like your idea, and we could also add a survey | Let us stop talking about your idea now
questions.correctAnswer: I like your idea, and we could also add a survey
questions.explanation: Building on a suggestion means accepting the good in it and adding something helpful. That keeps ideas growing and every teammate feeling valued.

questions.question: Nasra is starting a persuasive talk about recycling at school. Which sentence states her position most clearly?
questions.options: Recycling is a thing that exists in the world | Some people recycle and some people do not | I believe our school should recycle more, because it cuts waste | Today I will talk about a topic
questions.correctAnswer: I believe our school should recycle more, because it cuts waste
questions.explanation: A clear position statement says exactly what you believe and gives a reason. The other sentences describe the topic without taking any position.

questions.question: Ayaan wants to find out how the children in her class travel to school. What is the best way to collect this information?
questions.options: Guess, because she knows some of them | Look up how children travel in another country | Ask each classmate and record the answers in a tally chart | Ask only her best friend and stop there
questions.correctAnswer: Ask each classmate and record the answers in a tally chart
questions.explanation: To answer a question about your own class, collect answers from the whole class and record them carefully. Guessing or asking one person cannot show the full picture.

questions.question: Ayaan's tally chart shows: walking 12 children, bus 6 children, car 2 children. What does her data show?
questions.options: Nobody in the class walks to school | Most children in the class come by car | The same number use each way of travelling | Most children in the class walk to school
questions.correctAnswer: Most children in the class walk to school
questions.explanation: Comparing the numbers shows 12 is the biggest group, so walking is the most common way. Reading data like this is the first step of analysis.

questions.question: Why is 'our town has two markets' a fact rather than an opinion?
questions.options: Because a grown-up said it first | Because everyone likes markets | Because it is a short sentence | Because it can be checked and shown to be true
questions.correctAnswer: Because it can be checked and shown to be true
questions.explanation: A fact can be checked — you could visit the town and count the markets. An opinion, like 'markets are fun', tells you what someone feels instead.

questions.question: Sara has just finished making a poster about clean water. Which question helps her reflect on her learning?
questions.options: What new thing did I learn while making my poster? | Whose poster is the biggest in the class? | How many posters are there in the world? | Where should I hang the poster?
questions.correctAnswer: What new thing did I learn while making my poster?
questions.explanation: Reflection means looking back at your own learning. Asking what you learned, and what was easy or hard, helps you grow with every project.

questions.question: Three friends are building a model of their town together. What is the fair way to work?
questions.options: Each build a separate model in secret | Let one friend build it while the others watch | Share the tasks so everyone has a job to do | Argue about who is the best builder
questions.correctAnswer: Share the tasks so everyone has a job to do
questions.explanation: Working together means sharing the tasks so everyone takes part. The model gets better when every friend adds their effort and ideas.

questions.question: Omar is telling the class what his group found out about birds in the park. How should he present it?
questions.options: Talk about his favourite game instead | Speak clearly and show his picture so everyone can understand | Read as fast as possible to finish quickly | Whisper so only the front row can hear
questions.correctAnswer: Speak clearly and show his picture so everyone can understand
questions.explanation: Presenting findings means helping everyone understand what you discovered. A clear voice and a picture to point to make your message easy to follow.
